title: PostgreSQL vs. MongoDB Trade-offs
description: PostgreSQL vs. MongoDB Trade-offs. Interview-first coverage of modeling, invariants, transactions, indexing, and migration trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Choose storage based on access patterns, invariants, and change frequency.
Model embedded and referenced relationships in MongoDB.
Explain relational constraints, joins, transactions, and indexing trade-offs.
Plan a migration or polyglot boundary with clear data ownership and consistency rules.

mentalModel.text: Choose a database by data shape, invariants, and queries. PostgreSQL and MongoDB both support indexes and transactions, but their data models and query ergonomics differ. Neither is universally more scalable or more correct.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL fits relational data, foreign-key relationships, constraints, joins, and multi-row transactions. MongoDB is attractive when an aggregate is naturally document-shaped and read or updated together. Both can serve complex workloads; compare actual access patterns.

blocks.title: Workload signals
rows: Many cross-entity joins and relational constraints
Embedding can fetch a coherent aggregate

blocks.problem: An order contains customer, line items, prices, and payment state.
reasoning: List invariants such as valid customer references, positive quantities, and auditable state transitions.
Separate bounded order-owned data from shared entities.
Embed line-item price snapshots if appropriate while keeping shared relationships and constraints explicit.
blocks.outcome: Start with invariants and query patterns, not a blanket rule that one model always wins.

blocks.text: Embedding keeps related fields in one document and can make aggregate reads efficient and atomic. It becomes problematic for unbounded arrays, duplicated mutable data, or updates that must synchronize many copies. References avoid duplication but may require additional reads or lookups.

blocks.title: Order document example

blocks.text: A purchase-time price snapshot is deliberate denormalization, not a reason to duplicate the current product catalog everywhere.

PostgreSQL transactions are central for invariants across related rows. MongoDB supports single-document atomicity and multi-document transactions. For cross-service workflows, neither database makes an external side effect atomic; use an outbox, idempotency keys, or a saga where needed.

blocks.title: Conditional inventory update

blocks.problem: An order must decrement inventory and create an order record without overselling.
reasoning: Define the invariant and transaction boundary.
In PostgreSQL, use a transaction with a conditional update and check affected rows.
In MongoDB, keep the invariant in one document when practical, or use a transaction and test retry behavior.
blocks.outcome: Choose the model that makes the invariant enforceable and operationally understandable.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL supports B-tree and specialized indexes plus JSONB operators; MongoDB supports compound, multikey, text, geospatial, and other indexes. In both systems, indexes consume storage and increase write work. Flexible schema still needs validation and migration plans.

blocks.title: MongoDB compound index
blocks.source:
db.orders.createIndex({ tenantId: 1, createdAt: -1 })
db.orders.find({ tenantId: "t-42" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(50)

blocks.title: PostgreSQL JSONB index
blocks.source:
CREATE INDEX events_payload_gin ON events USING GIN (payload);
SELECT id FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"kind":"purchase"}';

blocks.text: Using two databases adds duplicated data, synchronization, monitoring, backups, access control, and incident ownership. Define one authoritative owner for each data domain and make derived copies explicitly rebuildable.

steps.title: Inventory access patterns
steps.description: Capture query shapes, constraints, volume, and latency SLOs.

steps.title: Define ownership
steps.description: Choose the authoritative system and change propagation path.

steps.title: Backfill and reconcile
steps.description: Copy in batches and compare counts, checksums, and invariants.

steps.title: Dual-run carefully
steps.description: Use an outbox or change stream with idempotent consumers.

steps.title: Cut over and rollback
steps.description: Switch gradually and retain a tested rollback path.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Avoid database-by-trend
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: A document database is not automatically faster, and a relational database is not automatically rigid. Choose based on access patterns and invariants.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Name the source of truth
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: If two datastores contain overlapping data, define which one owns updates and how derived copies are repaired.

revisionSheet.text: Choose by relationship patterns, invariants, and access patterns, not fashion.
Embed bounded aggregate data; reference unbounded or independently queried entities.
Both databases support transactions, but external side effects need explicit coordination.
Polyglot persistence adds ownership, synchronization, backup, and operational costs.

questions.prompt: A service relies on joins, foreign keys, and multi-row invariants across orders and payments. What is the strongest starting point?

options.text: PostgreSQL because relational queries and constraints fit
MongoDB because documents always eliminate joins
Redis because key-value storage guarantees foreign keys
A separate database for every table

questions.explanation: The relational model and declarative constraints align with this workload.

questions.prompt: An order has a bounded line-item list that must preserve purchase-time price. What MongoDB model is often reasonable?

options.text: Embed line-item snapshots in the order
Rewrite historical orders when current catalog price changes
Store each quantity in an unrelated database
Duplicate the entire current catalog in every order

questions.explanation: Embedding bounded order-owned snapshots keeps purchase-time values coherent with the order.

questions.prompt: A MongoDB document contains an array of millions of events queried independently by time. What is the concern?

options.text: An unbounded embedded array can grow inefficiently and complicate queries
MongoDB cannot index any array
PostgreSQL cannot store events
Every document must have one field

questions.explanation: Unbounded child collections often belong in their own collection with indexes based on access patterns.

questions.prompt: Which statement about transactions is accurate?

options.text: Both systems support transactions; data model and scope affect cost
MongoDB has no atomicity at any level
PostgreSQL cannot update multiple rows transactionally
A database transaction makes an external payment call atomic

questions.explanation: Both support transactions; external side effects need explicit coordination.

questions.prompt: A team chooses MongoDB for flexible schema. What must it still design?

options.text: Validation, document versioning, indexes, and migration strategy
Nothing because fields never change
A collection for every optional field
Equal byte length for every document

questions.explanation: Flexible storage still needs controlled contracts and evolution.

questions.prompt: A few JSON attributes need filtering while relational constraints remain important. What should be evaluated before adding a new datastore?

options.text: PostgreSQL JSONB with appropriate operators and indexes
Move all tables to a key-value store immediately
Store JSON only in logs
Remove constraints for performance

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL can combine relational structures with JSONB when query patterns fit.

questions.prompt: An order is committed to PostgreSQL and then an event is published. The process can crash between these steps. What addresses the gap?

options.text: Write an outbox record in the same transaction and publish idempotently
Assume the process never crashes
Increase SQL timeout
Store the event in ephemeral cache only

questions.explanation: The outbox couples the domain change and event intent; an idempotent worker publishes with retry.

questions.prompt: A team wants both PostgreSQL and MongoDB. What should be decided first?

options.text: Authoritative owner for each data domain and synchronization semantics
Which database has a more modern logo
How to dual-write without retries
How to skip reconciliation

questions.explanation: Clear ownership and synchronization prevent silent divergence.

questions.prompt: Which factors matter when choosing relational tables versus document modeling?

options.text: Relationship and join patterns
Required invariants and transaction boundaries
Whether related data is bounded and read together
The belief one database is universally more scalable

questions.explanation: Choose based on access patterns, invariants, and aggregate shape.

questions.prompt: Which can justify using both PostgreSQL and MongoDB?

options.text: Distinct workloads benefit from different models
Data ownership and synchronization are explicitly designed
The team can operate both systems reliably
Avoiding schema and migration planning

questions.explanation: Polyglot persistence can fit distinct workloads but adds operational complexity.

questions.prompt: MongoDB's flexible document model makes validation and schema evolution unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Flexibility makes validation and versioning more important, not less.

questions.prompt: Adding MongoDB without a distinct workload need can increase operational complexity without clear benefit.
questions.explanation: A second datastore adds synchronization, backup, security, monitoring, and ownership costs.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Design a marketplace with users, listings, bookings, payments, and flexible listing attributes.
strongAnswerPoints: Keep booking/payment invariants and relationships explicit.
Evaluate JSONB or a document store only for attributes whose access patterns justify it.
Define ownership, indexes, and operating costs before polyglot persistence.
pitfalls: Choosing MongoDB solely because attributes vary
Change one variable at a time and measure the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would map invariants and query patterns first. PostgreSQL is a strong default for bookings, payments, relationships, and constraints; JSONB may handle flexible listing attributes. I would add MongoDB only if a distinct document workload justified synchronization and operational overhead.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A team migrates a high-volume event collection from PostgreSQL to MongoDB. How would you make it safe?
strongAnswerPoints: Define source of truth and target shape, indexes, and validation.
Backfill in batches and replay changes idempotently.
Compare business invariants and cut over gradually with rollback criteria.
pitfalls: Uncontrolled dual writes and row-count-only validation
Change one variable at a time and measure the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would define ownership and mapping, backfill with progress tracking, replay changes idempotently, and compare both systems on real queries and invariants. I would shift traffic gradually and keep rollback available until reconciliation and latency are stable.
